\chapter{Night}
\label{ch:la-night}
\hlchaptermodality{29}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say night in Latin as nox, noctis, and see English night sitting inside it.}

Say nox and noctis, match it against English night, and build equinox out of aequus plus nox.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nox]{nox — English's own word, wearing a Roman toga}

\label{lesson:LA-C29-nox}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson gave \emph{diēs} its own moment. Here's its partner from \emph{media nox} — and this time, the English cousin isn't hiding behind centuries of sound change. It's staring you in the face.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nox — \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Nox} (genitive \textbf{noctis}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{} — is the word you've already met inside \textbf{media nox} (\textquotedblleft{}midnight,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 12).

\begin{cousinweb}
Trace \emph{nox} back far enough and you land on \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*nók\textsuperscript{w}ts}} — and this is about as solid a reconstruction as historical linguistics gets. The cognates read almost like the same word spelled differently across a dozen languages: English's own \textbf{night}, German \textbf{Nacht}, Greek \textbf{nyx}, Sanskrit \textbf{nakta}, Old Norse \textbf{nátt}, Gothic \textbf{nahts}. \emph{Nox} and \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} aren't just related — they're about as close to being the same word as two languages 6,000 years apart can get.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: The same suffix as diurnum, and a name for equal nights}]
Nox's own derivative, \textbf{nocturnus} (\textquotedblleft{}of the night\textquotedblright{}), wasn't built from scratch — it was coined \textbf{directly on the analogy} of \emph{diēs}'s own \textbf{diurnum}, reusing its exact \emph{-urnus} suffix on purpose: the same suffix-machine, deliberately applied to a second time-word. \emph{Nocturnus} gives English \textbf{nocturnal} and \textbf{nocturne} directly. And \textbf{aequus} (\textquotedblleft{}equal\textquotedblright{}) + nox's stem \emph{noct-} gives \textbf{equinox} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{equal night},\textquotedblright{} the day when day and night balance.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nox\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} genitive \emph{noctis}
  \item the tight cousin — nox/night, nearly the same word
  \item nocturnus's shared suffix with diurnum — the same -urnus pattern, two different times of day
\end{itemize}
